v. 
KYLE WAGNER, 
Defendant-Appellee.

 O R D E R 
Before: HERMANDORFER, Circuit Judge. 
Kyle Wagner is currently detained pending trial in the Eastern District of Michigan for one
count of cyberstalking and one count of interstate communications involving threats. See 18 
U.S.C. § 2261A(2); id. § 875(c).1 By decision issued on August 12, 2026, this Court determined 
that Wagner’s pretrial detention was warranted under the Bail Reform Act, 18 U.S.C. § 3142(g). 
Wagner now moves to recall this Court’s mandate and stay it pending the disposition of a petition 
for a writ of certiorari in the Supreme Court of the United States. Under 6 Cir. I.O.P. 41(b), this 
motion is referred “as a single-judge matter, to the judge who wrote the opinion.” 
Additional background on these proceedings is set out in this Court’s prior order, see D.E. 
10 (6th Cir. Apr. 3, 2026), and opinion, see United States v. Wagner, 187 F.4th 372 (6th Cir. 2026). 
By way of summary, this appeal arose after the district court reversed a magistrate judge’s 
detention order and released Wagner pending trial. The district court acknowledged that Wagner’s
charged conduct was “very serious” and that the Government had a “very strong argument that 
there was some protection of the public involved” in detaining Wagner. Id. at 380, 382 (quoting 
E.D. Mich., Detention Hearing Day 2 Tr., R.24, PageID 147, 149-50). But it reasoned that certain 
1 Wagner also faces a separate indictment in the District of Minnesota on charges including conspiracy to impede or 
injure a federal officer and solicitation to commit a crime of violence. See Indictment, R.1, pp. 2, 91 (No. 26-cr00115-KMM-DTS) (D. Minn. June 11, 2026).
Case: 26-1294 Document: 23 Filed: 09/28/2026 Page: 1
1a

No. 26-1294 
- 2 - 
release conditions—like requiring Wagner to promise that he would only use a few, designated 
internet devices and avoid making further online threats—could mitigate the risk Wagner 
presented to public safety. 
The Government appealed the district court’s release order and sought an emergency stay 
of that order pending appeal. A panel of this Court granted a stay, which resulted in Wagner’s 
detention through the course of the appellate proceedings. 
On August 12, 2026, this Court issued an opinion reversing the district court’s release 
order. See Wagner, 187 F.4th 372. The Court first noted that, since the 1985 decision in United 
States v. Hazime, 762 F.2d 34, our precedent implementing the Bail Reform Act has directed 
application of clear-error review for the district court’s “factual findings” and de novo review for 
the “ultimate question whether pretrial detention is warranted.” Wagner, 187 F.4th at 378
(brackets deleted) (quoting United States v. Stone, 608 F.3d 939, 945 (6th Cir. 2010) (citing 
Hazime, 762 F.2d at 37)). The Court then reasoned that the Government had carried its burden of 
proving Wagner’s dangerousness, citing, among other things, record evidence of Wagner’s 
doxxing attempt, “direct calls for violence against federal agents and their supporters,”2and 
communications with a Signal user about killing a former government official. Id. at 375, 379-83. 
Finally, the Court disagreed that the district court’s proposed conditions on Wagner’s internet use 
would sufficiently mitigate the relevant public-safety risks. Id. at 383-85. That conclusion 
followed from Wagner’s “particular history of internet activity” as well as from caselaw noting 
the potential inadequacies of electronic-access restrictions for online offenders. Id. 
Judge Bloomekatz dissented. She reasoned that Bail Reform Act appeals should trigger a 
more “deferential approach” to reviewing the district court’s “application of the facts to the pretrial 
detention standard.” Id. at 393 (Bloomekatz, J., dissenting). And she deemed that standard 
satisfied based upon, among other things, her understanding of the broader “context” of Wagner’s 
2 See Wagner, 187 F.4th at 37 (“[P]osts—appearing in the record verbatim—included calls for Wagner’s followers to 
‘put[] hands on’ ICE, ‘fight’ ICE, and ‘[g]et your f**king guns and stop’ ICE. In some of those posts, Wagner 
explained that he was ‘done with peaceful protests,’ that he was ‘not talking about peaceful protests anymore,’ and 
that it was ‘kill or be killed.’”) (citations omitted). 
Case: 26-1294 Document: 23 Filed: 09/28/2026 Page: 2
2a

No. 26-1294 
- 3 - 
online statements, Wagner’s lack of a “violent criminal history,” and the district court’s release 
conditions. Id. at 395, 398; see id. at 400-03. 
Wagner did not seek further review from this Court. And his trial is currently set to begin 
in early November 2026, though the parties have sought to continue that date. 
Consistent with the governing rules, see Fed. R. App. P. 41(b), the mandate issued on
September 3, 2026, see United States v. Wagner, No. 26-1294 (6th Cir. Sept. 3, 2026). On
September 18, 2026, Wagner filed a petition for a writ of certiorari in the Supreme Court seeking 
review of this Court’s decision and judgment ordering his pretrial detention. See Pet. for Writ of 
Cert., No. 26-391 (Sup. Ct. Sept. 18, 2026). He now moves this Court to recall and stay the 
mandate pending the Supreme Court’s disposition of his petition. See Fed. R. App. P. 41(d). That 
step, Wagner contends, is necessary before he can seek interim stay relief of the detention decision 
from this Court and the Supreme Court. 
Wagner did not seek to stay the mandate before its issuance. He thus “must overcome two 
hurdles if the relief requested is to be granted.” United States v. Holland, 1 F.3d 454, 455 (7th Cir. 
1993) (Ripple, J., in chambers). He must first show that this Court should recall the mandate now 
that it’s been issued; he then must justify a stay of that mandate. See id. 
Taking the recall request first, this Court has the inherent authority to recall its mandate. 
Patterson v. Haskins, 470 F.3d 645, 661-62 (6th Cir. 2006). But “such power should only be 
exercised in extraordinary circumstances because of the profound interests in repose attached to a 
court of appeals mandate.” United States v. Saikaly, 424 F.3d 514, 517 (6th Cir. 2005) (order). 
Exercise of this “last resort” power is justified only in the event of “grave, unforeseen 
contingencies.” Id. (quoting Calderon v. Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 550 (1998)). Examples include 
“‘fraud upon the court, clarification of an outstanding mandate, and correction of a clerical 
mistake.’” United States v. Murray, 2 F. App’x 398, 399-400 (6th Cir. 2001) (order) (quoting 
BellSouth Corp. v. FCC, 96 F.3d 849, 852 (6th Cir. 1996)). 
Wagner’s motion “does not fit into any of th[ose] categories.” BellSouth Corp., 96 F.3d at 
852. Nor does Wagner otherwise seek to justify his weekslong failure to seek any relief prior to 
Case: 26-1294 Document: 23 Filed: 09/28/2026 Page: 3
3a

No. 26-1294 
- 4 - 
the mandate’s issuance. That issuance, moreover, involved no “unforeseen” events; by virtue of 
this Court’s prior stay order, Wagner had remained detained pending the Government’s appeal. 
Still, Wagner reads this Court’s decisions to create a broader, catchall rule that permits 
recall of the mandate when a party’s petition for certiorari “was still pending at the time the motion 
to recall the mandate was filed with this court.” Wagner Recall and Stay Mot. 3. But Wagner’s 
cited cases, see id., don’t sweep that far. Each instead acknowledged that the “rare” scenario may 
warrant recall “based on [a] decision” of the Supreme Court or the court of appeals that works a
significant change in law affecting the rights of parties whose appellate proceedings are not yet 
final. Saikaly, 424 F.3d at 517-18 & n.2 (quoting Murray, 2 F. App’x at 400, in the course of 
denying recall); see United States v. Crawford, 422 F.3d 1145, 1146 (9th Cir. 2005) (recalling 
mandate for resentencing in light of pre-mandate issuance of “the Supreme Court’s decision in 
Blakely v. Washington”). 
Nothing like that happened here. Instead, Wagner took the routine step of petitioning for 
a writ of certiorari within the time allotted and after the Court’s mandate issued. If Wagner’s 
automatic-recall-when-cert-pending rule were right, scores of parties could sit idle through a 
mandate’s issuance and then later obtain recall by seeking cert. That rule would convert recalls 
from “contingencies” to a matter of course, Calderon, 523 U.S. at 550, contra the “strong public 
policy” in favor of the finality of judgments, BellSouth Corp., 96 F.3d at 851. And while Wagner 
counters that a recall here is warranted so that he can move for interim stay relief in the Supreme 
Court, there was another pathway well trodden by parties in his position: Timely move to stay the 
mandate, which triggers a delay of the mandate that allows for interim-relief requests. See Fed. R. 
App. P. 41(b), (d)(1); see also 16AA Wright & Miller’s Federal Practice & Procedure §§ 3987 
& 3987.1 (5th ed., supp. Apr. 2026) (collecting cases); Gressman, et al., Supreme Court Practice 
860-62 (9th ed. 2007) (collecting cases). 
Wagner’s failure to justify a recall of the mandate in turn forecloses this Court’s staying 
that mandate. Nor does Wagner’s case for a stay appear compelling on its own terms. To secure 
a stay pending the disposition of his cert petition, Wagner “must show that the petition would 
Case: 26-1294 Document: 23 Filed: 09/28/2026 Page: 4
4a

No. 26-1294 
- 5 - 
present a substantial question and that there is good cause for a stay.” Fed. R. App. P. 41(d)(1). 
“That is a daunting standard.” White v. Plappert, 137 F.4th 579, 581 (6th Cir. 2025) (quotation 
omitted). “Because stays issued pursuant to Rule 41 are tied to the certiorari process,” the Rule 
41 analysis “mirrors the Supreme Court’s own test for granting stays pending the filing of a petition 
for certiorari.” Id. Under that test, Wagner “must show (1) a reasonable probability that four 
Justices will consider the issue sufficiently meritorious to grant certiorari; (2) a fair prospect that 
a majority of the Court will vote to reverse the judgment below; and (3) a likelihood that irreparable 
harm will result from the denial of a stay.” Id. (quoting Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 
(2010) (per curiam)). The Rule 41 merits inquiry thus puts lower-court judges in an unnatural 
spot: We “must perform the predictive function of anticipating the course of decision in the 
Supreme Court of the United States” with respect to a circuit decision just issued. Books v. City 
of Elkhart, 239 F.3d 826, 828 (7th Cir. 2001) (Ripple, J., in chambers) (cleaned up). Judges are to 
do this by “consider[ing] the issues that the applicant plans to raise in the certiorari petition in the 
context of the case history” and “the considerations that guide the Supreme Court in determining 
whether to issue a writ of certiorari.” Id.; see also Sup. Ct. R. 10. 
Here, Wagner’s cert petition principally rests the case for Supreme Court intervention on 
the presence of a circuit split over which standard of review governs district courts’ detention 
decisions under the Bail Reform Act. Cert. Pet. 12-23. But the bulk of the cited divergence dates 
back to the mid-1980s. See id.; cf. Wagner, 187 F.4th at 379 (discussing Hazime, 762 F.2d 34). 
Such “staleness” often undercuts need for intervention, particularly without evidence of 
meaningfully different practical outcomes. See Gressman, et al., at 248 (“A stale conflict 
sometimes may suggest that the disagreement is not a recurring and important one.”); cf. Layne & 
Bowler Corp. v. W. Well Works, Inc., 261 U.S. 387, 393 (1923). Nor is it apparent that the split is 
as lopsided or stark as Wagner’s petition contends. The circuits generally apply clear-error review
to factual findings. And several circuits Wagner places in his pro-deference camp exercise 
“independent review tempered by deference,” Cert. Pet. 21-23—a standard presenting little 
apparent daylight with our de-novo-with-factual-deference approach. Wagner, citing the 
Case: 26-1294 Document: 23 Filed: 09/28/2026 Page: 5
5a

No. 26-1294 
- 6 - 
dissenting opinion, casts the standard of review as outcome determinative. Id. at 3-4. But the 
dissent’s core objection—over the meaning of what it viewed as ambiguous statements by 
Wagner—boils down to a factual disagreement that “does not implicate the circuit split” asserted. 
BP P.L.C. v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230, 246 (2021). 
All of those factors cut against the Supreme Court’s intervention, even spotting that splits 
can sometimes make a petition appealing. So do the problems with Wagner’s particular vehicle. 
Among them: the odds that his pretrial-detention claim will soon become moot, cf. Murphy v. 
Hunt, 455 U.S. 478, 481-82 (1982) (per curiam), as well as the wrinkle the independent indictment 
in Minnesota presents to the Government’s potential arguments for detention, Cert. Pet. 12 n.1; cf. 
18 U.S.C. § 3142(f)(2) (permitting reopening of detention record in light of new information).3
The final stay consideration requires balancing equities. Wagner has waived his Speedy 
Trial Act rights and agreed repeatedly to continue his trial date—from April, to July, to September, 
to November—and now jointly moves for another delay to early 2027. Cert. Pet. 35. Further, 
Wagner’s petition for certiorari represents that he “does not oppose further delay” of his trial “if 
necessary to ensure that this Court can adequately review the Sixth Circuit’s order prior to its 
expiration.” Id. It thus appears that Wagner has offered to voluntarily extend his detention to 
insulate his petition from mootness. Though detention usually constitutes irreparable harm, it’s 
dubious that the same treatment should extend to any “self-inflicted,” strategic extension of 
detention pending the disposition of Wagner’s petition for a writ of certiorari. Second City Music, 
Inc. v. City of Chicago, 333 F.3d 846, 850 (7th Cir. 2003). Conversely, the Government’s “law 
enforcement and public safety interests” weigh significantly in the equities calculus. Maryland v. 
King, 567 U.S. 1301, 1303 (2012) (Roberts, C.J., in chambers). 
3 Even if Wagner showed likely Supreme Court review, he would still face the task of demonstrating “a reasonable 
possibility that five [justices] will vote to reverse the judgment of this court.” Holland, 1 F.3d at 456.
Case: 26-1294 Document: 23 Filed: 09/28/2026 Page: 6
6a

No. 26-1294 
- 7 - 
For the above reasons, the motion for recall of the mandate and for a stay of the mandate
pending disposition of Wagner’s petition for a writ of certiorari is DENIED. 
ENTERED BY ORDER OF THE COURT
 Kelly L. Stephens, Clerk
